paragraphs: Dmitri jumped up in a sort of fury. He seemed suddenly drunk. His eyes went bloodshot all at once.
“And do you really mean to marry her?”

“At once, if she’ll have me. And if she won’t, I’ll stay all the same. I’ll be the porter at her gate. Alyosha!” he cried. He stopped short in front of him and, taking him by the shoulders, began shaking him violently. “Do you know, you innocent boy, that this is all delirium, senseless delirium? Because there’s a tragedy in it. Let me tell you, Alexey, that I may be a low man, with low and degraded passions, but a thief and a pickpocket Dmitri Karamazov can never be. Well, then—let me tell you that I am a thief and a pickpocket. That very morning, just before I went to beat Grushenka, Katerina Ivanovna sent for me. In strict secrecy (why, I don’t know; I suppose she had her reasons) she asked me to go to the chief town of the province and post three thousand roubles to Agafya Ivanovna in Moscow, so that nothing would be known of it here in town. So I had those three thousand roubles in my pocket when I went to see Grushenka, and that was the money we spent at Mokroe. Afterwards I pretended I’d been to the town, but I didn’t show her the post office receipt. I said I’d sent the money and would bring the receipt, and so far I haven’t brought it. I’ve forgotten it. Now what do you think you’ll say when you go to her today? ‘He sends his compliments,’ and she’ll ask you, ‘What about the money?’ You could still have said to her, ‘He’s a degraded sensualist and a low creature, with uncontrolled passions. He didn’t send your money then, but wasted it, because, like a low brute, he couldn’t control himself.’ But you might still have added, ‘He isn’t a thief though. Here are your three thousand; he sends them back. Send them yourself to Agafya Ivanovna. But he told me to say “he sends his compliments.”’ But as it is, she’ll ask, ‘But where is the money?’”
“Mitya, you’re unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t worry yourself to death with despair.”

“What, you think I’d shoot myself because I can’t get three thousand to pay back? That’s just it. I won’t shoot myself. I haven’t the strength now. Afterwards, perhaps. But now I’m going to Grushenka. I don’t care what happens.”
“And what then?”
“I’ll be her husband if she deigns to have me, and when her lovers come, I’ll go into the next room. I’ll clean her friends’ galoshes, get their samovar going, run their errands.”

“Katerina Ivanovna will understand it all,” Alyosha said solemnly. “She’ll understand how great this trouble is, and she’ll forgive. She has a lofty mind, and no one could be more unhappy than you. She’ll see that for herself.”
“She won’t forgive everything,” said Dmitri with a grin. “There’s something in it, brother, that no woman could forgive. Do you know what the best thing to do would be?”
“What?”
“Pay back the three thousand.”
“Where can we get it? Look, I have two thousand. Ivan will give you another thousand—that makes three. Take it and pay it back.”

“And when would you get hold of it, your three thousand? Besides, you’re not of age, and you must—you absolutely must—take my farewell to her today, with the money or without it, because I can’t drag on any longer, things have come to such a pass. Tomorrow is too late. I’m sending you to father.”
“To father?”
“Yes, to father first. Ask him for three thousand.”
“But, Mitya, he won’t give it.”
“As if he would! I know he won’t. Do you know what despair means, Alexey?”
“Yes.”

“Listen. Legally he owes me nothing. I’ve had it all from him; I know that. But morally he owes me something, doesn’t he? You know he started with twenty-eight thousand of my mother’s money and made a hundred thousand with it. Let him give me back just three of those twenty-eight thousand, and he’ll draw my soul out of hell, and it will atone for many of his sins. For that three thousand—I give you my solemn word—I’ll make an end of everything, and he’ll hear nothing more from me. For the last time, I’m giving him the chance to be a father. Tell him God Himself is sending him this chance.”
“Mitya, he won’t give it for anything.”

“I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well. Now especially. And that’s not all. I know something more. Only a few days ago—maybe only yesterday—he found out for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may really not be joking and really means to marry me. He knows her nature; he knows the cat. And do you suppose he’s going to give me money to help bring that about, when he’s crazy about her himself? And that’s not all, either. I can tell you more. I know that for the last five days he’s had three thousand drawn out of the bank, changed into hundred-rouble notes, packed into a large envelope, sealed with five seals and tied across with red tape. You see how well I know all about it! On the envelope is written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, in silence and in secret, and no one knows the money’s there except the valet, Smerdyakov, whom he trusts like himself. So now he’s been expecting Grushenka for the last three or four days. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent her word of it, and she’s sent him word that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her after that? Now you understand why I’m here in secret and what I’m watching for.”
“For her?”

“Yes, for her. Foma has a room in the house of these sluts here. Foma comes from our parts; he was a soldier in our regiment. He does jobs for them. He’s their night watchman, and in the daytime he goes grouse-shooting; that’s how he lives. I’ve set myself up in his room. Neither he nor the women of the house know the secret—that is, that I’m on the watch here.”
“So no one but Smerdyakov knows?”
“No one else. He’ll let me know if she goes to the old man.”
“So he was the one who told you about the money?”

“Yes. It’s a dead secret. Even Ivan doesn’t know about the money, or anything. The old man is sending Ivan to Tchermashnya on a two- or three-day trip. A buyer has turned up for the copse: he’ll give eight thousand for the timber. So the old man keeps asking Ivan to help him by going to settle it. It will take him two or three days. That’s what the old man wants, so that Grushenka can come while he’s away.”
“Then he’s expecting Grushenka today?”

“No, she won’t come today; there are signs. She’s certain not to come,” cried Mitya suddenly. “Smerdyakov thinks so, too. Father’s drinking now. He’s sitting at table with Ivan. Go to him, Alyosha, and ask for the three thousand.”
“Mitya, dear, what’s the matter with you?” cried Alyosha, jumping up from his seat and looking keenly at his brother’s frenzied face. For one moment the thought struck him that Dmitri was mad.
“What is it? I’m not insane,” said Dmitri, looking intently and earnestly at him. “Don’t be afraid. I’m sending you to father, and I know what I’m saying. I believe in miracles.”
“In miracles?”
“In a miracle of Divine Providence. God knows my heart. He sees my despair. He sees the whole picture. Surely He won’t let something awful happen. Alyosha, I believe in miracles. Go!”
“I’m going. Tell me, will you wait for me here?”

“Yes. I know it will take some time. You can’t go at him point-blank. He’s drunk now. I’ll wait three hours—four, five, six, seven. Only remember, you must go to Katerina Ivanovna today, even if it’s at midnight, _with the money or without the money_, and say, ‘He sends his compliments to you.’ I want you to say that line to her: ‘He sends his compliments to you.’”
“Mitya! And what if Grushenka comes today—if not today, then tomorrow or the next day?”
“Grushenka? I’ll see her. I’ll rush out and stop it.”
“And if—”
“If there’s an if, it will be murder. I couldn’t stand it.”
“Who will be murdered?”
“The old man. I won’t kill her.”
“Brother, what are you saying?”

“Oh, I don’t know.... I don’t know. Perhaps I won’t kill, and perhaps I will. I’m afraid he’ll suddenly become so loathsome to me, with his face at that moment. I hate his ugly throat, his nose, his eyes, his shameless snigger. I feel a physical revulsion. That’s what I’m afraid of. That’s what may be too much for me.”
“I’ll go, Mitya. I believe God will arrange things for the best, so that nothing awful happens.”
“And I’ll sit and wait for the miracle. And if it doesn’t come to pass—”
Alyosha went off thoughtfully toward his father’s house.
